ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Blood under the skin is the records' bodily image for someone who registers pain and itching, unlike unresponsive earth and wood.
EvidenceBody: It is consequently used by Gulin Qingmao as a qualification for people addressed in the hall: "you people must have blood under the skin" (汝諸人須是皮下有血始得), and "if he has blood under the skin, he will certainly have another livelihood" (他若皮下有血，必定別有生涯). A garden exchange also keeps the literal body image audible: seeing a cook cut melons, Yu'an Zhiji asks the head cook, "which one has blood under the skin?" (那個皮下有血). Zen bends the bodily phrase into a recurrent test for someone who registers a touch or blow, while the records themselves ground that use in pain and itching rather than an imported psychological category.
